title: Continuous learning: Filtering matters more than release chasing
desc: Uses networks and shared knowledge infrastructure to build contextual awareness while acknowledging anecdotal evidence and information overload.

kps.k: The cluster frames continuous learning as a practical capability for adapting to AI, rather than a race to follow every product release.
kps.d: The central proposition links informed experimentation, professional exchange and organisational change: lawyers need enough technical understanding to identify useful applications and retain judgment as tools evolve. Posner and Hron recommend repeated hands-on use to develop that understanding. Reyhani distinguishes access to technology from the training, deployment and change management needed to create value. These recommendations rest mainly on practitioner experience, not comparative evidence that particular learning methods improve legal outcomes.

qs.q: Zach (The LegalTech Fund) (22:23)  I mean, from an individual perspective, being experimenting with this stuff is… Because when you experiment with it, you understand what it can do, and then you can connect the dots in your head for how you can apply it in your day job.
qs.a: A Deep Dive into Legal Tech Investment with TLTF's Zach Posner · Market & press · 2025

qs.q: The more you do, the better your intuition becomes for where this is going and what impacts you think it might have on your teams, your talent, on the products you’re building, etc.
qs.a: Legal AI, Trust, and Agents: Joel Hron on Thomson Reuters, Anthropic, and the Future of CoCounsel · Legal-tech vendor · 2026

kps.k: Professional networks provide contextual intelligence, but their anecdotes do not independently validate market narratives.
kps.d: Boyko promotes exchanges among frontline lawyers; Buckley, Su and Gillespie use customer, partner and personal conversations to question media hype and competitive imitation. McIver and McDonnell also draw on internal specialists and customer feedback. These accounts explain how participants interpret developments and discover practical needs, not how they systematically establish adoption trends. Maziarek offers a complementary emphasis on surveys that expose providers to clients’ perspectives. The practical implication is to combine published analysis with situated experience while preserving the distinction between survey findings, commercial intelligence and anecdote.

qs.q: And so I always encourage frontline lawyers to see what other frontline lawyers are doing, that it is possible and get excited from that.
qs.a: Anastasia Boyko on Advisor Mode, Training Lawyers for the Post-Pyramid Firm · Law firms · 2026

qs.q: And so Andy and the other partners at Latitude will kind of give me anecdotes, will tell us like, hey, this is the conversation we’ve had with the GC or a law firm partner this week.
qs.a: Alex Su and Andy Chagui on Flexible Legal Talent, AI Pressure, and the Future of Law Firm Leverage · AI-native providers · 2026

kps.k: Learning beyond legal technology helps participants anticipate applications, although they disagree about how quickly capabilities translate into practice.
kps.d: Moon, Laskowski and McCormack look outside law because other sectors may reveal transferable uses earlier. Thompson points to software engineering; Williams teaches connections from applications to semiconductors; Lewis uses infrastructure and technology-business analysis to inform product planning and challenge vendor claims. A speaker in the Legora–Harbor discussion claims general-AI capabilities reach legal applications within weeks. That diffusion claim does not establish widespread use: Mostyn describes meaningful lawyer adoption as early, and Crutchfield sees mostly incremental applications. These are differences of emphasis and observation, not comparable measurements of a single adoption process.

qs.q: And I’ve said this before as well, but I find that following people who are not necessarily in legal is quite useful with this technology, because it’s surprising to me how much there is to learn from other disciplines that are maybe diving into use cases a little faster, and it turns out they’re not necessarily that different from us.
qs.a: How Small Law Firms and Solo Practitioners Can Harness Generative AI — full episode transcript · Regulators & courts · 2024

qs.q: So that’s one, I really, even my classes, we talk about, when we talk about AI, we talk about the whole stack, like from the application layer all the way down to semiconductors and, know, TSMC and at video, like these things are all related.
qs.a: Tiara Time and Data Center Politics: Vanderbilt’s AI Governance Playbook with Cat Moon and Mark Williams · Academia · 2026

kps.k: Information overload creates a tension between broad awareness, reliable filtering and time for actual work.
kps.d: Participants recommend podcasts, newsletters, social platforms and specialist commentators because these fit around existing workloads. McCormack sometimes relies on expert summaries rather than reading studies; Kercher uses Claude to explain research; Dave uses AI summaries before selectively returning to originals. Nguyen warns that chasing every trend can mean following marketing, while Steenhuis and Reichenberg caution against excessive news consumption. Platform preferences also diverge: Thompson values early discussion on X, whereas Steenhuis describes his community moving to LinkedIn. These personal practices support selective curation, not a ranking of channels by reliability or effectiveness.

qs.q: The technology is changing so quickly that by following a few smart thought leaders who get to focus on it full-time (while the rest of us have our full-time jobs), we can take advantage of some great shortcuts.
qs.a: Building an AI-Forward Law Firm: Lessons from Quinn Emanuel — full episode transcript · Law firms · 2025

qs.q: I want to get some of these things summarized, but then…  when I see something interesting, I’m able to actually click in and actually go to the actual source and actually take it a full read.
qs.a: Pit Crews, Seven C’s, and AI: Mirat Dave and Danish Butt from Swiftwater & Co. · Market & press · 2025

kps.k: Libraries and shared knowledge infrastructure could turn individual learning into organisational capacity.
kps.d: Laskowski connects information architecture, retrieval and curation to librarianship, while Marks anticipates a wider role for legal information professionals throughout the information life cycle. Proposed shared repositories would pool policies and practices, but volunteer commitment and contribution incentives remain unresolved. Dickinson adds operational requirements for AI-assisted current awareness: diverse sources, provenance, publisher relationships and human editorial review. His suggested audience-dependent accuracy thresholds are proposals, not measured performance. Together, these contributions extend the learning agenda beyond consuming news to maintaining trustworthy, reusable knowledge.

qs.q: A common use for AI systems is information retrieval, right knowledge expansion, and a key skill in the future as we wade through a quagmire of AI slop will be curation.
qs.a: Law Librarians Take the Lead: The Future of AI and Legal Information · Academia · 2025

qs.q: We say it’s really important and allows for human review before full sending.
qs.a: Vable's Matthew Dickinson on Current Awareness in the Age of GenAI · Legal-tech vendor · 2025

kps.k: AI education must develop legal reasoning and verification skills, not merely familiarity with interfaces.
kps.d: Dickason envisages mock trials and depositions accelerating junior development; Daves anticipates benefits from Shayesteh’s training project, and Vanderbilt participants describe tool building as a learning vehicle. None supplies measured learning outcomes here. Steenhuis identifies the countervailing problem: students must learn tasks that AI performs quickly but imperfectly so they can check its work. Lambert favours teaching through legal concepts and students’ own analysis. Black calls for preparation for technology-enabled solo practice and other roles. The unresolved question is how to preserve expertise while changing the activities through which novices acquire it.

qs.q: And I think we’ll see AI helping us train junior associates, then being able to do mock trials and all the rest very quickly, mock depositions, all of that.
qs.a: LexisNexis CTO Greg Dickason on Agentic Legal AI, Protégé, Shepard’s Verify, and the Future of Legal Work · Legal-tech vendor · 2026

qs.q: Quinten Steenhuis (34:33)  In academia, I think our big challenge is going to be how do we help people learn the things that they need to learn when there’s an AI that can do those things for them very quickly, but just not perfectly.
qs.a: From Legal Aid to LIT Lab: Quinten Steenhuis and the Builder’s Approach to AI · Academia · 2026

kps.k: Organisations should guide experimentation through strategy and support rather than rely on bans, symbolic adoption or indiscriminate purchasing.
kps.d: Butt recommends a two-year planning horizon backed by data preparation and knowledgeable staff; Posner calls for leadership commitment beyond IT. Leonard argues that organisations must shape employees’ existing AI use. Her supporting LinkedIn–Microsoft figures concern knowledge workers generally, not lawyers, and she qualifies both the sponsor’s interest and her recollection of strategy and training statistics. Gebauer similarly recommends supplying needed tools to reduce shadow AI. Practical priorities include relevant use cases, workflow-specific training, usable data and review of actual business value. Sam Moore’s warnings about context limits and usage-based overages add operational literacy to that agenda.

qs.q: And on the other end it’s like, okay, let’s try every tool under the sun and you get mediocre results because there’s no strategy.
qs.a: Pit Crews, Seven C’s, and AI: Mirat Dave and Danish Butt from Swiftwater & Co. · Market & press · 2025

qs.q: So I think that, I think there’s a whole mentality that comes with this and it needs some buy-in that’s not just coming from the IT side.
qs.a: A Deep Dive into Legal Tech Investment with TLTF's Zach Posner · Market & press · 2025

kps.k: Continuous adaptation does not resolve disagreement about employment, professional value or the limits of delegation.
kps.d: Dickason predicts faster development without fewer lawyers, linking demand to underserved legal needs; Su leaves associate numbers open; Nori anticipates disruption to Big Law demand and student prospects. These forecasts lack comparable employment evidence. Boyko, Shaver and Mostyn emphasise advice, trusted judgment and advocacy, while Hron anticipates governing delegated work. Samuels warns that excessive delegation could weaken legal craft and compromise; Luminance’s Eleanor instead envisages progressively removing review for routine agreements such as NDAs. Delimarsky explicitly declines precise forecasts. The shared preparation agenda therefore coexists with substantive uncertainty about which tasks remain human and how professional responsibility will operate.

qs.q: As clients understand how much AI tools can do, in-house teams will question why they’re hiring Big Law.
qs.a: Sateesh Nori Joins LawDroid: AI Tools for Access to Justice, Housing Court, and Legal Aid · Access to justice · 2026

qs.q: But I’ll say two things that I think about in a semi-worrying way are the loss of the art and the craft of being a lawyer, people delegating too much to these tools and losing the forest for the trees, or not paying attention to the why and the strategic calls.
qs.a: Anthropic’s Matt Samuels and Den Delimarsky - Claude & MCP: Building the USB-C for the Legal Tech Stack · Legal-tech vendor · 2026

vlens.an: The selected academia-and-research sources accept the proposition that continuous learning should prioritise contextual understanding, practical engagement and filtering over tracking every release. They materially extend it by specifying educational and institutional mechanisms: librarians can curate information and maintain shared knowledge infrastructure; students can learn through mission-aligned tool building; teaching can connect AI to legal reasoning and the wider technology stack; and collaborative workshops can turn individual learning into shared practice. Across the sources, preserving verification and professional judgment is a common reason for this approach, because learners must remain able to assess work that AI performs quickly but imperfectly. Material variation concerns emphasis rather than direction: some focus on collective curation and librarian-led infrastructure, others on experiential or full-stack education, and Steenhuis stresses selective professional networks and verification. The sources also acknowledge unresolved implementation issues, including contribution incentives, information overload and the risk that automation weakens skill acquisition. Their educational benefits are predominantly recommendations, aspirations and experiential judgments rather than measured outcomes. These curated sources should not be treated as representative of academia and research generally.

qs.q: A common use for AI systems is information retrieval, right knowledge expansion, and a key skill in the future as we wade through a quagmire of AI slop will be curation.
qs.a: Law Librarians Take the Lead: The Future of AI and Legal Information · Academia · 2025

qs.q: Use the tools, but when you talk about them, it’s from lawyering concepts, not “how to use the tool.”  Marlene Gebauer 31:06  Yes.
qs.a: Women + AI Summit, Real Talk: Leadership, Learning, and Not Letting “The Trap” Write Your Story · Academia · 2026

vlens.an: These access-to-justice and civil-society sources accept the cluster’s premise that AI adaptation requires continuing, contextual learning rather than indiscriminate release chasing, and they materially extend it by identifying constraints on who can adapt. Nori describes a mixed learning practice built from professional networks, informal conference exchange, newsletters and scholarship; his wider forecasts about legal education, employment and service-model disruption underscore why such learning matters, although they remain predictions rather than evidence of outcomes. Peterson shifts from individual learning to organisational capacity, arguing that scarce transition talent may especially hinder smaller and mid-sized firms. DiBona adds a separate strategic uncertainty: increasingly capable models may commoditise parts of the platform market, though he offers no comparative testing. The principal internal variation is therefore one of emphasis—Nori focuses on learning channels and preparedness amid anticipated market disruption, while Peterson and DiBona focus on resource constraints and technology-market uncertainty. These curated sources should not be treated as representative of the wider professional community.

qs.q: Sateesh Nori (39:41)  Surprisingly, LinkedIn is the best place I’ve found to learn and connect.
qs.a: Sateesh Nori Joins LawDroid: AI Tools for Access to Justice, Housing Court, and Legal Aid · Access to justice · 2026

qs.q: And also just the pace of change means there’s talent shortage and it’s hard to hire people to come into your firm, especially if it’s a smaller firm or even a mid-sized firm and help you with these transitions because labor is scarce.
qs.a: The Cytator Strikes Back: Kara Peterson & Rich DiBona On Descrybe’s Fresh Take on Legal Research · Access to justice · 2025

vlens.an: The selected traditional-law-firm sources accept the proposition that adaptation to AI requires continuous, selective learning rather than indiscriminate attention to every release. Their common rationale is practical constraint: lawyers must stay informed alongside full-time client work, so they rely on curated commentators, podcasts, newsletters, practitioner networks and AI-assisted explanations. They also value information grounded in use—frontline experimentation, broader technology developments and direct client perspectives—over undifferentiated market commentary. Collectively, they materially extend the proposition from individual learning into organisational practice: Nuara connects cross-sector monitoring to model and tool selection; Jones makes information governance, data location and workflow review part of adaptation; Maziarek adds surveys and client perspectives as a corrective to provider-side assumptions; and Boyko links practitioner exchange to recruitment and the preservation of advisory judgment. Material variation concerns emphasis rather than direction. Some sources prioritise fast, informal shortcuts through trusted experts; others stress frontier-model awareness, client intelligence, formal training, or governance and compliance. They also vary in confidence: some anticipate competitive and client-service benefits, while others foreground uncertainty and rapid change. These are practitioner recommendations and observations, not comparative evidence that the proposed learning methods improve adoption or legal outcomes, and this curated set should not be treated as representative of traditional law firms generally.

qs.q: The technology is changing so quickly that by following a few smart thought leaders who get to focus on it full-time (while the rest of us have our full-time jobs), we can take advantage of some great shortcuts.
qs.a: Building an AI-Forward Law Firm: Lessons from Quinn Emanuel — full episode transcript · Law firms · 2025

qs.q: And so the only thing I think we could say for sure is that there’ll be a tremendous amount of change and it’ll be a challenge to look at where data is stored, look at work processes, look at workflows.
qs.a: Exploring Legal Tech Innovations at ILTA Evolve 2025 with Josh Smith and Ken Jones · Law firms · 2025

vlens.an: The curated legal-tech vendor sources collectively accept the proposition that useful adaptation depends more on selective, practical learning than on tracking every release, and they materially extend it into product and organisational design. Common reasons include information overload and marketing noise; the greater value of hands-on experimentation, customer and practitioner networks, and external technology analysis; and the need to translate awareness into use-case selection, training, change management and workflow redesign. Several sources add concrete infrastructure and safeguards: curated or firm-owned knowledge systems, libraries and internal intelligence channels, source provenance, human verification, task-specific benchmarks, drift testing, governance across multiple tools, and routing questions to appropriate services. Material variation remains. Some advocate broad monitoring of general AI because capabilities may transfer quickly into law, while others deliberately limit news consumption or return to fundamentals. Some focus primarily on learning networks, whereas others emphasise technical infrastructure, evaluation or strategic deployment. Views also differ on delegation: Samuels warns that it may erode legal craft and judgment, while Luminance’s Eleanor speculates that human review of routine agreements could eventually diminish. A small subset addresses uncertainty or market developments without enough evidence to establish a position on the filtering proposition. Across the sources, most claims are practitioner observations, product accounts or forecasts rather than comparative evidence that these learning methods improve legal outcomes; the curated set should not be treated as representative of legal-tech vendors generally.

qs.q: For all the geeks out there in LegalTech I do want everyone to take a breath and to look at what we have, which is profound technology, and to start to deliver value rather than jumping from hype cycle to hype cycle.
qs.a: RAG is Not Dead: Josef's Sam Flynn on Legal Tech That Works · Legal-tech vendor · 2025

qs.q: I’ll start by saying our platform turns a firm’s documents and matter history into a private, curated knowledge graph that the firm owns and runs inside its own environment.
qs.a: Own the Graph: Stephen Costigan on Private AI, Knowledge Infrastructure, and Law Firm Advantage · Legal-tech vendor · 2026

vlens.an: The curated market-analyst, consultancy and press sources broadly accept the proposition that useful continuous learning depends on selective, contextual engagement rather than following every release. Their common reasons are practical: product proliferation and competitive imitation make announcements unreliable proxies for value; information volume requires trusted commentators, summaries and selective return to original sources; and effective adoption depends on hands-on experimentation, firm-specific strategy, leadership support and continuing governance. Collectively, they materially extend the proposition by translating individual learning into organisational practices—competitive intelligence for buy-in, AI-assisted knowledge synthesis, support designed to reduce shadow AI, and governance treated as an evolving capability. There is meaningful internal variation. Posner prioritises repeated experimentation, while Black, Shaver, Glassmeyer, Dave and Butt emphasise curation through varied or trusted networks. Gebauer and Lambert add cross-industry learning and shared knowledge infrastructure. Crutchfield stresses incremental present-day gains and uncertain payoff, whereas Shaver and Black forecast faster strategic or structural change. One brief Shaver excerpt merely promotes competitive analysis and does not clearly address filtering. Across these sources, recommendations and forecasts are mainly qualitative, anecdotal or product-based rather than comparative evidence that particular learning practices improve legal outcomes; the sources should therefore not be treated as representative of all analysts, consultancies or press commentators.

qs.q: And on the other end it’s like, okay, let’s try every tool under the sun and you get mediocre results because there’s no strategy.
qs.a: Pit Crews, Seven C’s, and AI: Mirat Dave and Danish Butt from Swiftwater & Co. · Market & press · 2025

qs.q: Being able to synthesize all of this and surface all of it for different types of work is becoming important.
qs.a: From AI Personas to Rogue Agents: Rethinking Legal Training, Security, and Value · Market & press · 2026

vlens.an: The AI-native legal-provider sources support the proposition that adaptation to AI depends on continuous but selective learning rather than indiscriminate release chasing. Su and Chagui combine trade coverage with recurring conversations among clients and provider partners, using practitioner anecdotes to test whether published narratives reflect operational reality. Mazares similarly favours curated alerts, regular reading and exchanges with trusted industry contacts, while warning against complacency and confident long-range prediction. Both accounts treat networks as sources of contextual intelligence, not systematic validation, and their recommendations are grounded mainly in professional experience rather than measured comparisons of learning methods. Material variation lies in emphasis: Su and Chagui focus on cross-checking market claims and anticipating changes in law-firm leverage, whereas Mazares adds AI-assisted news curation and links learning to people, process and measured procurement. Young merely directs listeners to Garfield AI materials and a judicial speech, so his excerpt does not establish a position on filtering, information overload or continuous learning. These sources are a curated selection and should not be read as representative of AI-native legal providers generally.

qs.q: But really what I always worry about is that when I read things in Bloomberg or ALM, I don’t know if it’s tied to reality.
qs.a: Alex Su and Andy Chagui on Flexible Legal Talent, AI Pressure, and the Future of Law Firm Leverage · AI-native providers · 2026

qs.q: I think having conversations with people in the industry that we trust is a great way to learn.
qs.a: Greg Mazares Sr. on AI, E-Discovery, and the Future of Human-Led Legal Services · AI-native providers · 2026

vlens.an:
This curated set of regulator-, court- and professional-body-oriented sources supports the proposition that useful AI adaptation depends more on selective, contextual learning than on tracking every release. The recurring reasons are practical: legal professionals have limited time, can become overwhelmed by platform churn, and can learn more efficiently through curated commentary, expert networks, shared use cases and insights from disciplines adopting AI more quickly. Several sources also connect continuous learning to action: organisations should guide employee experimentation already under way, while judges should understand and monitor AI without surrendering professional judgment to it.

There is material variation in emphasis. McCormack and Leonard primarily advocate accessible education, cross-disciplinary learning, aggregation and everyday experimentation; Leonard further predicts that platform-by-platform comparison will recede as AI becomes embedded in existing practice software. Their organisational argument relies partly on explicitly caveated survey figures about knowledge workers generally, not legal-sector-specific evidence. Judge Schlegel places greater weight on democratic accountability, creator bias and keeping judicial judgment in control, while combining informal monitoring with established institutional resources. Across the set, the support is chiefly normative, experiential and predictive rather than comparative evidence that particular learning channels improve legal outcomes. The sources therefore support rather than materially extend the cluster synthesis, and their selection should not be treated as representing all regulators, courts or professional bodies.

qs.q: But just to counter that or temper it a little bit, I would also say that I expect that this era where we’re all trying to find the different platforms in their most recent iterations—and which one compares to the others—will end at some point (or at least recede in its importance).
qs.a: How Small Law Firms and Solo Practitioners Can Harness Generative AI — full episode transcript · Regulators & courts · 2024

elens.an: The 2023–2024 sources support the proposition that adapting to generative AI requires continuous but selective learning, not exhaustive tracking of every release. Their common rationale is practical: lawyers face information overload and limited time, so they should use curated commentary, accessible professional conversations and lessons from faster-moving nonlegal disciplines to build enough contextual awareness to identify relevant applications. They also treat adaptation as organisational rather than purely individual: because employees may already be experimenting, organisations should provide strategy and guidance instead of waiting or leaving use unmanaged. Material variation lies in emphasis. Some passages focus on helping risk-averse lawyers catch up and on cross-disciplinary resources; another predicts that platform comparison will matter less as AI becomes embedded in existing practice software; and another stresses governing employee-led experimentation. The evidentiary basis is limited: most claims are recommendations, personal experience or predictions. The cited adoption figures concern knowledge workers generally, are qualified for sponsor interest and uncertain recollection, and do not establish legal-sector adoption or learning outcomes. These curated sources therefore support the cluster’s practical framing without demonstrating that the recommended learning methods are comparatively effective.

qs.q: But just to counter that or temper it a little bit, I would also say that I expect that this era where we’re all trying to find the different platforms in their most recent iterations—and which one compares to the others—will end at some point (or at least recede in its importance).
qs.a: How Small Law Firms and Solo Practitioners Can Harness Generative AI — full episode transcript · Regulators & courts · 2024

qs.q: So you have an opportunity to shape how they use it—or they’re just going to go rogue and use it however they think is most helpful.
qs.a: Transforming Law with AI: Generative Models, Innovation in Dispute Resolution, and Leadership in Change — full episode transcript · Regulators & courts · 2024

elens.an:
The curated 2025 sources collectively accept the proposition that effective adaptation depends on selective, contextual learning rather than following every release, and materially develop it into an organisational operating model. Common reasons include limited professional time, information overload, vendor hype and rapid technological change. Sources therefore favour hands-on experimentation tied to defined use cases; filtering through trusted specialists, customers, peers and cross-disciplinary analysis; and converting individual awareness into durable capacity through libraries, shared knowledge hubs, current-awareness systems, governance, usable data, training and leadership support. Several contributions add concrete safeguards—human review, source diversity and provenance, task-specific benchmarks, drift testing, verification and controlled source access—while process-led accounts recommend prioritising workflow steps with the greatest operational value and deferring low-impact novelty.

Material variation concerns pace, evidence and the limits of delegation. Some sources claim that general-AI capabilities reach legal applications within weeks or predict widespread agentic adoption, whereas others describe current legal-AI applications as incremental, lawyer adoption as nascent, or benefits as prospective. Learning practices also vary between informal shortcuts—podcasts, summaries and professional networks—and formal organisational infrastructure. Networks are valued for context but remain anecdotal rather than independent validation of market trends. Most sources preserve human judgment and verification, but Luminance’s speculative vision of progressively removing review for routine contracts creates tension with that safeguard-oriented emphasis. A few excerpts merely identify developments or resources to monitor and are insufficient to establish a position. These differences do not reverse the overall direction: the period extends the proposition from a learning preference into a strategy for governed adoption at scale. Because the corpus is curated, this synthesis characterises these sources only and does not indicate how prevalent the position was across the legal sector in 2025.

qs.q: I just kind of believe that if you chase every new trends and new publications going out there, you essentially will chase the marketing cycle.
qs.a: Trust at Scale: Nam Nguyen on How TruthSystems is Building the Framework for Safe AI in Law · Legal-tech vendor · 2025

qs.q: So your third recommendation is, is centralized knowledge hub for sharing of resources like policies and best practices.
qs.a: Law Librarians Take the Lead: The Future of AI and Legal Information · Academia · 2025

elens.an:
The curated 2026 sources collectively accept the proposition that adapting to legal AI requires continuous, selective and practice-oriented learning rather than indiscriminate release tracking. Common reasons include the speed and volume of AI developments, the limited value of hype or symbolic adoption, and the need to connect technical awareness to concrete workflows, client needs and retained professional judgment. Sources repeatedly favour hands-on experimentation, trusted professional networks, direct customer and practitioner intelligence, curated commentary, and learning from developments outside legal technology. They also consistently qualify these practices as experiential or anecdotal rather than validated measures of adoption or learning effectiveness.

The period materially develops the proposition in several ways. Costigan, Hron and Gebauer move from individual awareness to organisational knowledge infrastructure through curated firm-owned knowledge graphs, agent-specific access to legal content and broader knowledge synthesis. Lambert, Gebauer, Steenhuis, Dickason and the Vanderbilt participants specify educational methods: teaching through legal reasoning, collaborative workshops, simulations, tool-building and continued verification. Maziarek adds surveys and direct client perspectives as a partial corrective to anecdotal professional intelligence, while Mazares and others connect learning to procurement review, cost literacy, workflow selection and change management.

Internal variation concerns emphasis rather than rejection. Some sources advocate broad, cross-sector monitoring, including frontier models, software engineering and semiconductor infrastructure; others deliberately limit news consumption or disconnect from it to protect time for substantive work. Platform preferences differ, with some valuing X for early signals and others moving toward LinkedIn or established institutional resources. Sources also disagree about downstream employment and delegation: Dickason expects faster lawyer development without fewer lawyers, Su leaves associate numbers open, and Nori predicts substantial disruption, while Samuels and Schlegel stress retaining legal or judicial judgment. One flexible-staffing source does not directly address filtering or learning and is therefore unclear, but it does not oppose the proposition. These disagreements reinforce the synthesis’s caution that continuous adaptation cannot itself settle contested forecasts about professional roles. Overall, the 2026 material builds on the proposition by supplying concrete educational, governance and knowledge-infrastructure approaches, while leaving their comparative effectiveness largely unmeasured.

qs.q: I’ll start by saying our platform turns a firm’s documents and matter history into a private, curated knowledge graph that the firm owns and runs inside its own environment.
qs.a: Own the Graph: Stephen Costigan on Private AI, Knowledge Infrastructure, and Law Firm Advantage · Legal-tech vendor · 2026
